did_you_know.text: In the ancient Near East, purple and scarlet dyes were costly, so using them expressed importance and honor. Tekhelet was generally made from a valuable blue dye.

The cubit was an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the fingertips, though its size varied. The Tabernacle’s measurements were therefore given in a unit familiar to people of that time.
Cloth made from goat hair was commonly used for tents in the ancient Near East. It was flexible and fairly durable, making it suitable as an outer layer for a portable tent.
The curtains were not meant only to cover the top; part of them extended beyond the walls. This gave better protection from sun, wind, and rain.
The exact identity of the animal called “tachash” in the Torah is unknown. That is why translations suggest different kinds of animal skin, and the question remains open.
Shittah wood comes from acacia trees, which can grow in hot, dry regions. Acacia wood is known for its durability, making it suitable for construction in the desert.
The sockets were heavy bases on which the boards stood. Using silver for them both strengthened the structure and gave it a dignified appearance.
The bars served as reinforcing beams that connected the boards. This made the walls a stable system rather than just a row of separate panels.
The middle bar ran from end to end through the boards, functioning like a central lengthwise beam. Such a design helped distribute pressure across the wall.

The phrase “Holy of Holies” is an example of an intensive Hebrew expression: literally, “the holy place of the holy places,” meaning the most holy place. A similar pattern appears in phrases such as “Song of Songs.”
Placing the table and the menorah on opposite sides created a fixed order inside the Tabernacle. Such organization was especially useful in a structure that could be taken down and set up again.

The terms “skilled work” and “embroidered work” probably refer to two different textile techniques, though their exact meanings are not completely certain. This shows that the Tabernacle required several kinds of craftsmanship, not just simple sewing.
